 Jordan Rosenfeld Sat, October 31, 2026 at 1:00 PM EDT 4 min read South_agency · Getty Images Election-year headlines can make it tempting for small business owners to anticipate tax changes before they happen. However, tax professionals said the more useful approach is to get the business financially organized, confirm compliance obligations and make decisions using the rules currently in effect — not campaign promises or predictions. 
 What should business owners actually focus on before year-end? Tax experts point to several practical moves that can help shore up finances, avoid costly mistakes and leave businesses better prepared for what's to come.

 1. Close Your Books and Recheck Estimated Taxes 
 Accurate, current books give owners a real picture of their year-to-date profit, which is essential for estimating taxes and deciding whether a final estimated payment may be needed. 
 Lea D. Uradu, JD, a tax attorney at FileTax.com , said owners should "complete the books by the current month, in order to know the year-to-date profit, rather than guessing." 
 She said tax-planning decisions should begin with a clear estimate of the business's total tax bill. 
 Business owners should "do the work that pays off no matter who wins," according to Joseph Rios, an IRS enrolled agent (EA) with Civita Tax Solutions . "Then compare that profit to the estimated tax you've paid so far. If you're behind, the January 15, 2027, payment is your last chance to catch up for 2026." 
 For many pass-through business owners, that payment is the final estimated-tax deadline for 2026. However, owners who underpaid earlier in the year could still owe an underpayment penalty. 
 2. Review the Records That Support Your Tax Return 
 Before year-end gets busy, owners should "check three things," Rios said. First, that every bank and card account is reconciled through last month. Second, that owner withdrawals and personal charges are kept out of business expenses. Third, that estimated tax payments are recorded as payments, not expenses. 
 "Then compare this year's income to last year's. That tells you whether your estimated payments still cover you," he added. 
 Uradu said owners should also "verify that the entity is current with the state and that all annual filings, licenses and registrations are current." 
 3. Get Payroll, Contractors and Sales Tax in Order 
 Don't leave complex reporting or sales-tax collection or worker classification to the end of year. 
 Story Continues "Avoiding legal exposure is best started with worker classification," Uradu said, including determining whether workers are employees or independent contractors. 
 Rios urged owners to collect paperwork early to make 1099 filing easier. 
 "If you run payroll, make sure your payroll provider's year-to-date totals match your books before W-2 season. And if you collect sales tax on materials, book it as money you owe the state, not as income." 
 Businesses selling online or across state lines may have sales-tax registration and collection obligations depending on where they do business and the rules in each state. 
 4. Watch Official Policy Developments, Not Campaign Promises 
 Tax rules do not change because of an election result, a speech or a news alert. Even when legislation is introduced or passed, its final terms and effective dates may differ from what owners expected. 
 "What a business owes is only defined by current law," Uradu said. 
 She said owners of pass-through businesses may want to track updates on deductions that affect how their income is taxed, as well as provisions with expiration or phase-down dates. 
 5. Avoid Big Moves Made Only for a Potential Tax Change 
 Election speculation is not a sound reason to restructure a business, alter hiring plans or make a major purchase, both experts cautioned. It can lead to timing and cash flow problems. 
 For example, Rios said, "Don't buy a truck in December just because of something you heard about a tax bill. A deduction only saves you a share of the price. You still pay the rest." 
 Buy equipment when the business needs it, and plan around the rules in effect today, not the ones in the news. 
 A clean set of books and a current-law plan can put owners in a stronger position to respond if policy changes actually arrive.
